extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and research-integrity professionals interested in retractions and scientific misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Coverage and critique of how journals, publishers, and institutions handle allegations of fabricated data, retractions, expressions of concern, and citation of retracted work, using the Yoshitaka Fujii case as a running example.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPE retraction notice standards / quality of retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘15% of retraction notices for the affected papers fail fully to meet standards from the Committee for Publication Ethics (COPE). Many lacked appropriate language and requisite watermarks stating that the articles had been removed, and some have vanished from the literature.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices should follow COPE standards: use clear, appropriate language explaining the reason for retraction; mark retracted articles (e.g., watermarks) so they remain clearly flagged in the literature and do not disappear. Failures include vague wording, lack of visible notice/watermark, or removal without trace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and diligence in retracting problematic papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated concern that journals and publishers have been slow or spotty in responding to clear evidence of fabrication (e.g., ‘What took more than five years? Elsevier retracts 20 papers…’; ‘Why did it take so long?’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers, editors and institutions should act promptly when credible evidence of misconduct emerges: investigate, issue expressions of concern if needed, and retract when warranted. Long delays undermine the literature and may put patients at risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding citation of retracted work ('zombie papers')
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: ‘An anesthesiology journal has retracted a 2018 paper that cited three retracted papers by Yoshitaka Fujii… journals had a spotty record in reacting to the Fujii scandal…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors should screen references for retracted or unreliable sources. Journals should correct or retract articles that rely on or cite retracted work; failure to do so is negligence and perpetuates 'zombie' citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical analyses to assess data plausibility (Carlisle-style scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘An anesthesiologist used statistical tools to determine the odds the results were likely to have come from actual experiments. The answer: infinitesimally small.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statistical tests and forensic methods to detect improbably consistent or implausible data distributions (e.g., Carlisle analyses). Extremely low probabilities for observed results are strong evidence warranting further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigation and formal committee review
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of institutional inquiries: ‘A committee investigated approximately 40 publications… and “identified ten publications with clear ethics violations”’ and university reports that tie up loose ends and recommend retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should convene independent committees to review allegations, document findings, and recommend corrective actions (expressions of concern, retractions, disciplinary measures). Institutional reports should be transparent and used to update the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author accountability and separate examination of collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Society recommended retractions for a co-author of Fujii; investigations examined publications by Yuhji Saitoh, many of which did not include Fujii, concluding some likely fabricated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should assess the contributions and responsibilities of co-authors; co-authors may be held accountable and subject to retraction recommendations if evidence indicates ethical violations in publications they are named on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Expressions of Concern (EOCs) as interim editorial action
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where journals issued expressions of concern (EOCs) for papers (e.g., Wiley journals issued EOCs before retracting four papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When credible concerns arise but an investigation is ongoing, journals should issue EOCs to alert readers while preserving the record; EOCs should be clear about the nature of the concern and updated with outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for appropriate ethical/IRB approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories and reporting highlight ‘lack of IRB approval’ as an issue in the Fujii case and related misconduct investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical research must have documented ethical approval (IRB/ethics committee). Absence of IRB approval is a serious red flag and may justify expressions of concern or retraction if ethical oversight was absent or misrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher and editorial responsibility to clean the literature and communicate actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple posts document publishers (Elsevier, Wiley, Springer) retracting papers, issuing statements, and sometimes being criticized for slow or inadequate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editors are responsible for coordinating corrections and retractions, ensuring notices meet standards, maintaining permanent, discoverable records of retractions, and communicating clearly with readers and indexing services to prevent ongoing citation of problematic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern detection and heightened scrutiny for recurrent anomalous publication profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations found patterns (e.g., Fujii: ‘In 2012 ... falsified data in 172 of 212 papers… 126 involved randomized controlled trials’), suggesting systemic issues rather than isolated errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a single author or group shows a high rate of problematic publications or implausible results, editors and institutions should apply heightened scrutiny across that author’s corpus (statistical re-analysis, audit of raw data, broader review) rather than treating each paper in isolation.
